function.name: calculate_electric_current
function.description: Calculate the electric current through a conductor given voltage and resistance. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

voltage.description: The voltage across the conductor in Volts. This is a float type value.

resistance.description: The resistance of the conductor in Ohms. This is a float type value.

conductance.description: The conductance of the conductor in Siemens. Optional if resistance is provided. Default: 0.3 This is a float type value.

message.content:
Electricity isn’t something that was “discovered” by a single person—rather, it’s a natural phenomenon that has been observed and studied for millennia. Here’s a quick overview of some key figures who helped turn those observations into the science we know today:

| Person | Contribution |
|--------|--------------|
| **Thales of Miletus** (c. 600 BCE) | First recorded observation of static electricity by rubbing amber (Greek *elektron*). |
| **William Gilbert** (1544–1603) | Coined the term *electricus* and distinguished between magnetism and static electricity in his book *De Magnete*. |
| **Benjamin Franklin** (1706–1790) | Conducted the famous kite experiment, proving that lightning is electrical and introduced the concept of positive and negative charges. |
| **Alessandro Volta** (1745–1827) | Invented the voltaic pile (the first battery), providing a steady source of electric current. |
| **Hans Christian Ørsted** (1777–1851) | Discovered the relationship between electricity and magnetism (electromagnetism). |
| **Michael Faraday** (1791–1867) | Developed the principles of electromagnetic induction, laying the groundwork for electric generators and motors. |
| **James Clerk Maxwell** (1831–1879) | Formulated Maxwell’s equations, unifying electricity, magnetism, and light into a single theoretical framework. |

So while no single individual “discovered” electricity, the cumulative work of these and many other scientists turned ancient observations into the modern field of electromagnetism.
